The Lowland paca (Cuniculus paca) is a large, caviomorph rodent inhabiting Neotropical forests from southern Mexico to northern Paraguay, where it plays a significant role as a seed predator and disperser. While foraging primarily on fallen fruits and seeds, this species exhibits a relatively slow life history for a mammal of its size. Under the normothermic conditions typical of resting endotherms at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], females experience a gestation period lasting 116 days [tg = 116 days], which is notably prolonged compared to many other rodents of similar body mass. This extended gestation is likely linked to the production of precocial offspring, an uncommon trait among rodents that contributes to the species’ low reproductive output but high neonatal survival. At parturition, neonates emerge at a substantial wet weight of 680 grams [Wwb = 680 grams], an impressive starting mass that equips them for rapid independence. This substantial birth weight positions the newborn as one of the largest among caviomorph neonates, reflecting a maternal investment strategy geared toward producing well-developed, mobile young capable of evading predators shortly after birth.

Pups remain dependent on their mother for a period of milk ingestion and early growth before transitioning to solid food. Nutritional emancipation occurs when young reach a wet weight at weaning of 2700 grams [Wwx = 2700 grams], a milestone that represents a fourfold increase from the birth mass. The suckling juvenile is nursed for approximately 78 days after birth [tx = approximately 78 days after birth] under the thermal conditions of maternal normothermy at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], a duration that allows the offspring to accumulate substantial lipid reserves before being left to fend for itself. Following weaning, the juvenile experiences a period of accelerated somatic growth and behavioral refinement, during which it gains the skills necessary for independent survival in a predator-rich environment. This post-weaning phase is critical for achieving a body size sufficient to escape gape-limited predators and to compete for high-quality fruit patches on the forest floor.

Sexual maturation in female Lowland pacas is a gradual process that does not culminate in first reproduction until a considerable amount of time has elapsed since birth. Puberty, defined as the onset of estrous cyclicity and ovarian activity, occurs at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. This relatively late maturation for a rodent of moderate size is consistent with the species’ overall slow life-history schedule, which prioritizes high juvenile survival over rapid turnover. Females do not usually breed until they have attained a sufficiently large body frame to support gestation and lactation. Consequently, the age at first reproduction often coincides closely with the age at which adult body size is approached, ensuring that maternal resources are adequate for the production of well-developed precocial young. This reproductive strategy aligns with that of other large-bodied caviomorphs such as agoutis and capybaras.

Adult body size in Cuniculus paca is among the largest observed in the family Cuniculidae, with individuals achieving a maximum asymptotic mass. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is approximately 11,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 11,000 grams], a figure that aligns with the range of 6 to 12 kilograms frequently cited in field guides for this species. This substantial adult mass is accompanied by a moderate basal metabolic rate; respirometry trials conducted on resting individuals at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C] have recorded a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 2746.8 milliliters per hour [JOi = 2746.8 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate is relatively low for a mammal of its mass, reflecting an energy-conserving lifestyle that reduces food requirements and allows the species to thrive on a diet of scattered, seasonally abundant fruits. The combination of a low metabolic rate and a large body size is typical of Neotropical forest frugivores.

Reproductive output in the Lowland paca is constrained by the lengthy gestation and the prolonged period of maternal care. Field studies indicate that females produce two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter] and, under normothermic conditions at 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], typically achieve a maximum of 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = 1.5 litters per year]. This relatively low annual fecundity is offset by the high survival probability of the precocial offspring, which are mobile and capable of consuming solid food within days of birth. The lifespan of this species is comparatively long for a rodent; marked individuals in captivity have been known to survive for 16.3 years [am = 16.3 years] under the stable thermal conditions that maintain a core body temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C]. This extended longevity, combined with delayed maturation and small litter sizes, situates Cuniculus paca at the slow extreme of the mammalian slow-fast continuum, a life-history strategy that is viable only in relatively stable, low-mortality environments.
